## Overview

::: {.callout-important}
## Two Key Tasks Today

1. **Form your project group** (3–4 students) — this is your group for the Research Report
2. **Begin your literature review** — searching for papers related to your project topic

You **must** attend this lab. If you don't attend and haven't signalled your intent to participate, you will be allocated to a group on Monday of Week 17.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Research Plan Due Tomorrow
Your **Research Plan** is due **Friday 27 February, 12 noon** via Learn. This is your first assessed submission. See the [assessment brief](../../assessments/research-plan.qmd) for details.
:::

---

## Part 1: Group Formation (20 min)

### Forming Your Group

Your group will work together for the rest of the term to design and run a study. Each member will then write their own individual Research Report (due 1 April) using the group's shared data.

**Group size:** 3–4 students

**What your group will do together:**

- Develop your research methodology (Week 17)
- Create your procedure and materials (Week 18)
- Collect data (Week 19)
- Analyse data (Week 20)

**What you do individually:**

- Write your own Research Report (2,000 words, due 1 April)

### Self-Check: Understanding Group Work

**1. The Research Report is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>A group submission</option><option value='answer'>An individual submission using group data</option><option value=''>Optional</option><option value=''>Due before Easter</option></select>

**2. You should share with your group members:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Your written report draft</option><option value='answer'>Data collection responsibilities and raw data</option><option value=''>Your introduction paragraphs</option><option value=''>Your reference list only</option></select>

**3. If two group members submit very similar reports, this is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Expected since they used the same data</option><option value=''>Fine as long as the data is the same</option><option value='answer'>An academic misconduct concern — reports must be independently written</option><option value=''>Only a problem if they have the same hypothesis</option></select>

True or False: Every group member must write their own report, even though the data is shared. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: You can copy your group member's Introduction as long as you change a few words. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

---

### Group Agreement

Once you've formed your group, discuss and agree on:

::: {.callout-note}
## Group Setup Checklist
- [ ] Exchange contact details (email, phone, WhatsApp)
- [ ] Set up a group communication channel
- [ ] Agree on when you can meet outside of labs
- [ ] Discuss expectations — how will you divide the work?
- [ ] Note each member's name and student number
:::

---

## Part 2: Your Project Topic (15 min)

Your group will receive a project topic from your lab tutor. Each topic involves a simple experiment that can be analysed with an independent-samples or paired-samples t-test.

### Understanding Your Topic

Once you have your topic, work through these questions with your group:

**1. An independent variable (IV) is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>What you measure</option><option value='answer'>What you manipulate or compare</option><option value=''>The result of the study</option><option value=''>The participant's age</option></select>

**2. A dependent variable (DV) is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>What you manipulate</option><option value='answer'>What you measure as the outcome</option><option value=''>The number of participants</option><option value=''>The type of design</option></select>

**3. In a between-subjects design:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Each participant does all conditions</option><option value='answer'>Different participants are in each condition</option><option value=''>There is no control group</option><option value=''>The IV is measured, not manipulated</option></select>

**4. In a within-subjects design:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Each participant does all conditions</option><option value=''>Different participants are in each condition</option><option value=''>Only one condition is used</option><option value=''>The DV changes between groups</option></select>

### Your Project Variables

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

**For your project topic, identify:**

**What is the independent variable?**
<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>I can identify my IV and its levels</option><option value=''>I think I know but I'm not sure</option><option value=''>I need to ask my tutor</option></select>

**What is the dependent variable?**
<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>I can identify my DV and how it's measured</option><option value=''>I think I know but I'm not sure</option><option value=''>I need to ask my tutor</option></select>

**What type of design will you use?**
<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Between-subjects</option><option value=''>Within-subjects</option><option value='answer'>My project documents specify the design</option></select>
:::

---

## Part 3: Literature Searching (25 min)

Now that you have your topic, it's time to find relevant published research. This will form the basis of your Introduction section.

### Where to Search

**1. The best starting point for psychology-specific research is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Google</option><option value='answer'>PsycINFO via the Goldsmiths Library</option><option value=''>Wikipedia</option><option value=''>ChatGPT</option></select>

**2. Google Scholar is useful because:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>It only shows peer-reviewed papers</option><option value='answer'>It covers many disciplines and shows citation counts</option><option value=''>It's the same as PsycINFO</option><option value=''>It writes summaries for you</option></select>

**3. To access full-text articles through Goldsmiths, you should:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Pay for each article</option><option value='answer'>Use the library's database access or set up Google Scholar Library Links</option><option value=''>Only read abstracts</option><option value=''>Search on general Google instead</option></select>

### Search Strategy Practice

Your group should now search for papers on your topic. Try the following:

**4. Boolean AND is used to:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Find either term</option><option value='answer'>Require both terms to appear</option><option value=''>Exclude a term</option><option value=''>Search for an exact phrase</option></select>

**5. Putting quotation marks around a phrase (e.g., "free recall") means:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The words can appear separately</option><option value='answer'>The exact phrase must appear together</option><option value=''>The phrase is excluded</option><option value=''>It searches titles only</option></select>

**6. If your initial search returns 5,000+ results, you should:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Read them all</option><option value=''>Give up on that topic</option><option value='answer'>Add more specific terms or apply filters</option><option value=''>Only look at the first page</option></select>

**7. If your search returns very few results, you should:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Conclude there's no research on the topic</option><option value='answer'>Try broader or alternative search terms</option><option value=''>Submit your report without references</option><option value=''>Only use textbook citations</option></select>

### Practice Search

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try This Now
1. Go to [Goldsmiths Library](https://www.gold.ac.uk/library/) and access PsycINFO
2. Search for terms related to your project topic
3. Try at least **three different search term combinations**
4. Aim to find **3–5 relevant papers** as a group
:::

True or False: Wikipedia is an acceptable source for your Research Report reference list. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: A paper published in 2010 can still be a useful source if it's highly cited and relevant. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

---

## Part 4: Evaluating and Recording Sources (20 min)

### Reading Papers Strategically

You don't need to read every paper cover to cover. Read strategically:

**1. When you first find a paper, you should read:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The entire paper carefully</option><option value='answer'>The abstract first, to check relevance</option><option value=''>Only the results</option><option value=''>The reference list</option></select>

**2. The Introduction of a paper is most useful for:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Finding statistical results</option><option value='answer'>Understanding background theory and finding other relevant papers</option><option value=''>Learning how to do the analysis</option><option value=''>Checking the sample size</option></select>

**3. The Method section of a relevant paper helps you because:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>You can copy their procedure</option><option value='answer'>It shows how similar studies have been designed and measured the DV</option><option value=''>It tells you what results to expect</option><option value=''>It's not useful for your project</option></select>

**4. A peer-reviewed source means:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>It was published online</option><option value=''>The author is a professor</option><option value='answer'>Independent experts evaluated it before publication</option><option value=''>It has been cited many times</option></select>

### Recording What You Find

For each paper you find, record:

::: {.callout-note}
## Source Record Template
For each relevant paper, note:

1. **Full reference** (authors, year, title, journal)
2. **What they studied** (research question / hypothesis)
3. **How they studied it** (design, participants, key method details)
4. **What they found** (key results, effect sizes if reported)
5. **Why it matters for your project** (how does it connect to your topic?)
:::

### Self-Check: Source Quality

**5. Which of these is the STRONGEST source for your Introduction?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>A newspaper article about memory research</option><option value=''>A YouTube lecture on the topic</option><option value='answer'>A peer-reviewed journal article reporting an experiment</option><option value=''>A textbook chapter on general psychology</option></select>

**6. How many quality sources should you aim for in your Introduction?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>1-2</option><option value=''>3-4</option><option value='answer'>5-8</option><option value=''>As many as possible</option></select>

True or False: You should only cite papers that support your hypothesis. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: Reading the reference lists of relevant papers is a good way to find more sources. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

---

## Part 5: From Sources to Hypothesis (10 min)

### Developing Your Hypothesis

Based on the literature you've found, you should be able to start forming a hypothesis.

**1. A hypothesis should be:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Vague and general</option><option value='answer'>Specific, testable, and directional (or explicitly non-directional)</option><option value=''>Based on what you hope will happen</option><option value=''>The same as the research question</option></select>

**2. "Concrete words will be recalled better than abstract words" is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>A research question</option><option value='answer'>A one-tailed (directional) hypothesis</option><option value=''>A two-tailed hypothesis</option><option value=''>A null hypothesis</option></select>

**3. Your hypothesis should be based on:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Your personal opinion</option><option value=''>What would be most interesting</option><option value='answer'>What previous research suggests is likely</option><option value=''>What's easiest to test</option></select>

### Group Discussion

::: {.callout-note}
## Discuss With Your Group
1. Based on the papers you've found, what does the literature suggest?
2. What direction do you predict your results will go?
3. Is your hypothesis one-tailed or two-tailed? Why?
4. How does your hypothesis connect to the theory you've read about?
:::

True or False: A hypothesis must always predict a specific direction of effect. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: Your hypothesis should be informed by previous research, not just a guess. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

---

## Summary

::: {.callout-important}
## What You Should Have Done Today

- [ ] Formed a group of 3–4 students
- [ ] Exchanged contact details and set up a communication channel
- [ ] Received your project topic
- [ ] Identified your IV, DV, and design
- [ ] Searched PsycINFO and/or Google Scholar for relevant papers
- [ ] Found at least 3–5 potentially relevant sources
- [ ] Started recording key information from each source
- [ ] Begun discussing a hypothesis based on the literature
